lesson.title: Additive Increase, Multiplicative Decrease: TCP Reno's Full Loop
lesson.summary: TCP Reno combines slow start, congestion avoidance, fast retransmit, and fast recovery into a single algorithm whose long-run behavior is a repeating sawtooth of gradual growth and sharp cutback known as AIMD.
lesson.body:
Each of the previous four chapters described one piece of a machine. TCP Reno is that machine assembled: it is the specific combination of slow start for the initial aggressive ramp-up, congestion avoidance for the steady linear growth once near capacity, fast retransmit for detecting loss quickly via duplicate ACKs, and fast recovery for responding to that kind of loss without a full collapse. Reno was a significant refinement over its predecessor, TCP Tahoe, which had slow start and congestion avoidance but treated every loss, whether detected by duplicate ACKs or by a timeout, as cause for a full reset to slow start. Reno's insight was that loss detected by duplicate ACKs is a milder event than loss detected by a timeout, and the two deserve different responses.

Reno therefore branches on how loss is discovered. If three duplicate ACKs arrive, fast retransmit fires, and fast recovery halves the congestion window and continues from there without ever revisiting slow start. If instead the retransmission timer expires with no ACK at all, that is treated as a much stronger signal of serious congestion (or an outright break in the path), and Reno responds the way Tahoe always did: ssthresh is set to half the current window, and cwnd is reset all the way down to its minimum, restarting slow start from scratch. This distinction matters because a timeout usually means duplicate ACKs never arrived either, which in turn usually means nothing at all is getting through right now, a very different situation from one lost segment amid an otherwise flowing stream.

The overall pattern this produces is called AIMD, additive increase, multiplicative decrease. During congestion avoidance, the window grows by roughly one segment per round trip, an additive increase. When loss is detected via duplicate ACKs, the window is cut by half, a multiplicative decrease, rather than dropping to a fixed additive amount. This choice of decrease rule is not arbitrary: it can be shown that additive increase paired with multiplicative decrease converges toward a fair and efficient split of a shared bottleneck's capacity among competing flows, whereas other combinations, such as multiplicative increase with additive decrease, do not converge to fairness in the same way. This is part of why AIMD became the foundation for decades of TCP congestion control, even as later algorithms replaced pieces of it.

Trace a full cycle to see the sawtooth. A connection starts in slow start with cwnd = 1, growing 1, 2, 4, 8 across successive RTTs until it hits ssthresh = 8, at which point it shifts to congestion avoidance and grows 9, 10, 11, 12 across subsequent RTTs. Suppose at cwnd = 12 a segment is lost and detected via triple duplicate ACK. Fast retransmit resends it immediately, and fast recovery sets ssthresh to 6 and cwnd to roughly 9 (6 plus 3 for the duplicate ACKs already seen), then deflates to 6 once the retransmission is acknowledged. Congestion avoidance resumes from cwnd = 6, growing 7, 8, 9, and so on, until the next loss event triggers another halving. Graphed over time, cwnd rises in a straight line, drops sharply by half, rises in a straight line again, drops again: the sawtooth is the visible signature of AIMD in action, and it is what nearly all subsequent loss-based congestion control algorithms, including the CUBIC algorithm covered next, were designed to refine rather than replace.
